score.name: BXP, INC.
score.moat_justification: Real but narrow: scarce premier gateway locations, the largest premier-workplace platform in the US and a proven development engine are genuine advantages, and the current leasing cycle (occupancy 88.4% and rising, 91.3% leased) shows tenants paying up for the best buildings. But the filed evidence caps the score: gross margin has fallen four straight years to 59.1%, the measurable roic_proxy was only 8.5-8.7% (FY2016-17), GAAP ROE ran 0.3-5.4% in FY2023-25, and the model is capital-hungry ($953M TTM capex) and heavily levered. That is a moderate 5/10, not the sustained well-above-cost-of-capital record a 7+ requires.

description.text: BXP, a Delaware corporation, is a fully integrated, self-administered and self-managed REIT, and it is one of the largest publicly-traded office REITs (based on total market capitalization as of December 31, 2025) in the United States that develops, owns and manages primarily premier workplaces. BXP was formed in 1997 to succeed the real estate development, redevelopment, acquisition, management, operating and leasing businesses associated with the predecessor company founded by Mortimer B. Zuckerman and Edward H. Linde in 1970. Our properties are concentrated in six dynamic gateway markets—Boston, Los Angeles, New York, San Francisco, Seattle and Washington, DC. At December 31, 2025, we owned or had joint venture interests in a portfolio of 179 commercial real estate properties, aggregating approximately 52.6 million net rentable square feet of primarily premier workplaces, including eight properties under construction/redevelopment totaling approximately 3.5 million net rentable square feet. analysis_md:
# BXP — BXP, Inc. (Boston Properties)

Pass-1 run, 2026-10-20, engine release 5.5.0. All figures below are copied from key_numbers.md, dcf_numbers.json, ttm.json, financials_history.csv or fundamentals.json — none are recomputed. Filing figures quoted from the FY2025 10-K balance sheet (filed 2026-02-27) are labelled as such; market/quarter colour is from the Q2 2026 reporting covered in the research searches.

## What it is
The largest publicly traded developer, owner and manager of premier workplaces in the United States — a REIT (SIC 6798) holding trophy office and life-science assets in six gateway markets (Boston, New York, San Francisco, Seattle, Washington, DC, Los Angeles), plus an active development pipeline (290 Binney Street delivered in 2026, 343 Madison Avenue under construction). SIC sector Real Estate → SECTOR_MODEL_MISMATCH: the OE/capex DCF fits REITs poorly, confidence is low and the name ranks under sector misfits.

## Owner's earnings
**FY2025 (10-K via EDGAR, from financials_history.csv):** operating cash flow $1,245,157,000; capex $900,437,000 — the sum of the two filed captions, PaymentsToAcquireOtherProductiveAssets $683,750,000 + PaymentsForCapitalImprovements $216,687,000 (capex_provenance in dcf_numbers.json); SBC $44,334,000 (always a real cost).
- **Conservative owner's earnings FY2025: $300,386,000 = $1.89/share** (oe_conservative / oe_per_share in the CSV).
- Maintenance version (NI + D&A − min(capex, D&A) − ΔNWC): $288,451,000 — same ballpark, which raises confidence in the conservative figure.
- OE positive 5 of the last 5 fiscal years, but falling: FY2023 $552,655,000 ($3.52/sh) → FY2024 $349,539,000 ($2.22/sh) → FY2025 $300,386,000 ($1.89/sh). The driver is capex, not operations: OCF was $1,301,520,000 / $1,234,501,000 / $1,245,157,000 across FY2023–25 while capex climbed $697,387,000 → $841,013,000 → $900,437,000 (development completions plus leasing capital).
- statements.json's owner's-earnings row reads higher ($517,073,000 for FY2025) because its capex line carries only the single PaymentsToAcquireOtherProductiveAssets caption ($683,750,000) and omits the $216,687,000 capital-improvements line. The CSV / engine figure is the complete one and is the figure of record.
- Consolidated OE includes the share belonging to noncontrolling interests (operating-partnership units and property partnerships); the per-share figures are struck on common diluted shares (158,869,000 latest), so the common holder's claim is slightly thinner than the headline — immaterial against a verdict this far below the hurdle.
- Dividends paid were $643,107,000 in FY2025 (fundamentals.json) — more than twice conservative OE of $300,386,000. A REIT distributes out of FFO (which adds back $912,088,000 of D&A), not out of OE; on the OE definition the payout is not covered, which is the model's standing complaint about the sector, not a liquidity claim.

**Base used = TTM owner's earnings through Q2 2026, from ttm.py (filing-direct, no hand math):**

- Capex: FY $900,437,000 − prior YTD $407,698,000 + current YTD $460,510,000 = **TTM $953,249,000** (both filed captions in every leg)

It is the most current and the most conservative of the three, so it is the base; the median is retained in the reporting.

## Moat: 5/10 — moderate, narrow
Justification: scarce premier gateway locations, the largest premier-workplace platform in the US and a proven development engine are real advantages, and the current leasing cycle shows tenants paying up for the best buildings. But the filed evidence caps the score: gross margin has fallen four straight years, measurable ROIC was only high-single-digit, GAAP ROE ran 0.3–5.4% in FY2023–25, and the model is capital-hungry and heavily levered. That is not the sustained well-above-cost-of-capital record a 7+ requires.
- FOR: Irreplaceable premier-workplace locations in six gateway markets — scarcity, zoning and replacement cost keep competing new supply slow; scale and integration (largest US premier-workplace owner/developer/manager; 290 Binney, 570,000 sq ft fully leased to AstraZeneca, delivered ahead of schedule and under budget); leasing momentum and visibility (~1.8M sq ft leased in Q2 2026, 29% above the 10-year quarterly average; occupancy up three straight quarters to 88.4%; leased rate 91.3% with most commencements due before year-end 2026); pricing power in the tightest submarkets (asking rents rising sharply at trophy assets such as 510 Madison and 680 Folsom, with AI-driven demand building).
- AGAINST: Hybrid work is a secular demand headwind — occupancy was still only 88.4% in Q2 2026, six years after the pandemic; gross margin eroded from 62.8% (FY2021) to 59.1% (FY2025 and TTM, fundamentals.json) — no demonstrated pricing power at portfolio level; returns are thin (roic_proxy measurable only in FY2016–17 at 8.7% / 8.5% because the filer's operating-income tag stops after FY2017; GAAP ROE 3.2% / 0.3% / 5.4% in FY2023–25); capital intensity ($953,249,000 TTM capex; management expects 2026 leasing capital alone nearer $500M); leverage ($15,633,220,000 of debt on the FY2025 10-K balance sheet against a $9,391,540,935 market cap — refinancing at higher rates is a standing drag, with interest expense up from $579,572,000 in FY2023 to $653,138,000 in FY2025, fundamentals.json).
- A 5 gives CAP = 8.5 years: growth holds 2 years, then converges linearly to the 2.5% terminal rate over 8.5 years, 15-year projection.

The bull (7.66%) and super-bull (14.66%) starts are above every revenue print, deliberately: OE here is a thin residual ($280,277,000 TTM on $1,284,500,000 of OCF), so capex normalization alone — TTM capex of $953,249,000 falling back toward FY2023's $697,387,000 as developments deliver — mechanically lifts OE far faster than revenue can grow. ## Flags — every fragility flag resolved
- **STALE_FY** (latest FY ended 9.6 months ago): resolved by construction — the base is the TTM figure from ttm.py through Q2 2026, legs quoted above. The TTM SBC warning is also resolved here: ttm.json's current-YTD leg uses the reconciled AllocatedShareBasedCompensationExpense figure ($41,500,000 vs ShareBasedCompensation $41,057,000, +1.1% — tag-rounding scale, recorded in ttm.json sbc_reconciled_legs) while the FY and prior-YTD legs use ShareBasedCompensation; each leg is the filer's total stock compensation for its period, and the $443,000 tag difference cannot move a $280,277,000 OE total.
- **NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE** (2023, 2024, 2025): structural REIT depreciation, not a one-off tax or working-capital item. Net income of $190,215,000 / $14,272,000 / $276,800,000 is struck after D&A of $830,813,000 / $887,191,000 / $912,088,000, which OCF adds back; episodic non-cash impairment charges sit on top (e.g. the Q1 2024 Shady Grove impairment, $0.08/share in the company's Q1 2024 release). The OCF-based conservative OE is the series used throughout, so the divergence does not contaminate the base — it is exactly why a REIT's GAAP earnings line is unusable and its FFO line exists.
- **SECTOR_MODEL_MISMATCH** (Real Estate): accepted. Confidence is **low**, and the name ranks under sector misfits. The standing policy (Andrew, 2026-10-15) sizes the final tier one notch below the numbers tier. There is no notch below D: F is a different verdict, meaning no positive normalized OE, and BXP's normalized median is $2.22/sh with OE-positive years 5/5. So tier_override stays null and the final tier is D. The quantified REIT lens: FY2026 FFO guided at $6.99–$7.05/share puts the $59.115 price at roughly 8.4x guided FFO, and Q2 2026 FFO was $1.78/share with occupancy at 88.4% — a REIT-multiple argument that is kinder than the OE lens, but even the super-bull OE scenario returns only 9.19%, so no lens on file supports 15% at this price.
- **WIDE_SCENARIO_SPREAD** (super-bull IV 4.52x super-bear IV): real — OE is a thin, capex-driven residual, so the outcome range IS wide. Confidence is low (never high with this flag) and the verdict is sized to the conservative end.
- **BIG_NET_CASH** (net cash 2.61x normalized OE): **false — a debt-tag artifact, resolved against the filing.** The engine's net_debt_basis is CURRENT_ONLY:CommercialPaper: its debt tags caught only the $750,000,000 of commercial paper. The FY2025 10-K consolidated balance sheet (in thousands, as filed) shows mortgage notes payable, net $4,280,067; unsecured senior notes, net $9,806,100; unsecured term loans, net $797,053; unsecured commercial paper $750,000; unsecured line of credit $0 — $15,633,220,000 of debt in total, against cash and cash equivalents of $1,478,206,000 and total liabilities of $18,473,924,000 (the total-liabilities figure matches financials_history.csv exactly). On the filing basis BXP carries roughly $14.16B of net debt — heavy leverage, the opposite of a cash pile. In this engine debt feeds diagnostics only (the OE paths are already after interest: interest expense of $653,138,000 in FY2025 is inside net income and OCF), so the misread does not inflate the IV or the tier; it only voids the −2.61x leverage diagnostic, which this analysis replaces with the filing figures above.

## My thoughts / overlay
- The honest headline is the base choice, and here it does not matter: preliminary run on the normalized median base ($2.22/sh) printed weighted IRR 6.72% and IV@15% $19.59; the final TTM-base run prints 5.76% and $15.10. Both are Tier D by a wide margin — the method range is D to D.
- What the OE lens is really saying: at $59.115 the market is paying for the buildings (asset value, FFO multiple, occupancy recovery), not for the residual cash flow after the capex those buildings continuously demand. FY2023–25 capex of $697M → $900M against flat OCF is the whole story; if deliveries (290 Binney done; 343 Madison under construction) let capex fall while the 91.3% leased rate converts to occupancy, OE/share can rebound fast — that is the bull case, and it still only earns 6.83%.
- Balance sheet is the risk the OE paths understate: $15,633,220,000 of debt, a dividend of $643,107,000 paid in FY2025 against $300,386,000 of conservative OE, and an asset-sale program ($1.2B+ of proceeds since the 2025 investor day, per Q2 2026 reporting) explicitly aimed at deleveraging. Management also cut the quarterly dividend to $0.70 ($2.80/yr, from $3.92/yr) — capital discipline, but an admission that the prior payout outran cash generation.
- Quality is not the debate: premier assets, occupancy inflecting up three straight quarters, AI-driven tenant demand in exactly BXP's markets. Price versus owner's earnings is the debate, and it is not close.
